## Purpose

**How well does a normal/lognormal model describe different asset classes, and which financial conclusions depend on it?**

This is a two-hour formative laboratory. Nothing is submitted for marks. Complete the tasks in this worksheet and retain the rendered HTML as a record of your work.

You will estimate models, diagnose their departures from the data, examine correctly calibrated tests, and explore a jump scenario. The four series are the same investments as in Week 1:

| Series | Exposure | Investor currency |
|---|---|---|
| Equities | VWRL.AS, global equities | EUR |
| Bonds | IEGA.AS, euro government bonds | EUR |
| Gold | PHAU.L, physical gold converted from USD | EUR |
| Portfolio | 60% equities, 30% bonds, 10% gold | EUR |

The supplied returns use the lecture's frozen 2020–2025 data. They are **nominal total returns**, without safe-account discounting or transaction costs. The portfolio resets its weights at each common observation. This differs from the excess-return calculations and transaction-cost exercise in Week 1.

## Working with AI

Continue the Week 1 workflow:

1. State the financial question and predict one feature of the answer.
2. Request one small piece of R code.
3. Read and explain it before running it.
4. Check definitions, units and numerical identities.
5. Interpret the result in your own words.

Use the supplied R reference for function names and assumptions. Ask AI to simplify any code you cannot explain. Never accept a model merely because a function runs or a p-value is large.

<details class="concept">
<summary>Why must portfolio simple returns be weighted before taking logs? Click after writing your answer.</summary>
<div class="answer"><p>A weighted sum of simple returns follows from the self-financing wealth calculation with starting weights. The log is nonlinear, so averaging component log returns generally gives a different portfolio return.</p></div>
</details>

**Interval convention.** “Daily” means one common trading-observation step. Weekends and exchange holidays can make its calendar length exceed one day. Monthly data use non-overlapping end-of-month wealth ratios, starting with February 2020. The first incomplete month is excluded.

## Task 2: Fit a benchmark and calculate investment outcomes

For each daily series, estimate the normal log-return parameters using

$$
\widehat m=\bar r,\qquad
\widehat s=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(r_i-\bar r)^2}.
$$

**Predict first:** will the asset with the largest daily standard deviation also have the largest fitted one-day VaR?

For initial wealth $V=\text{EUR }100{,}000$ and $\alpha=99\%$, calculate:

$$
E[R]=e^{\widehat m+\widehat s^2/2}-1,\quad
\operatorname{median}(R)=e^{\widehat m}-1,\quad
P(R<0)=\Phi(-\widehat m/\widehat s),
$$

$$
L=-VR,\qquad
\operatorname{VaR}_{.99}(L)
=V\left[1-\exp\{\widehat m+\widehat s\,\Phi^{-1}(.01)\}\right].
$$

These are **one-day model outcomes**, meaning one common observation step. Use daily estimates directly; no annualisation is needed. The lecture's numerical VaR example was one year, so its amounts should not match this table.

1. Build one row per series with $n$, $\widehat m$, $\widehat s$, fitted mean and median simple returns, loss probability and VaR.
2. Use `normal_outcomes()` to check your direct calculations for at least one series.
3. Verify that fitted mean simple return is at least fitted median simple return.
4. Compare the observed simple returns with the fitted lower 1% quantile. Report the fraction falling below it.

<details class="concept">
<summary>Does a fitted 99% VaR mean that larger losses are impossible?</summary>
<div class="answer"><p>No. Under the continuous fitted model, 1% of losses exceed this threshold. Historical exceedances here use the same sample as the fit, so they are an in-sample diagnostic, not a forecast validation.</p></div>
</details>

## Task 4: Tests, asset classes and observation frequency

The reference hypothesis is that observations are IID normal with unknown mean and variance. The core tests are:

| Test | Discrepancy | Reference used here |
|---|---|---|
| Shapiro–Wilk | Ordered sample values relative to normal order statistics | R's normality-test implementation |
| Jarque–Bera | Skewness and kurtosis | Asymptotic chi-square with 2 degrees of freedom |
| Anderson–Darling | Weighted CDF differences, emphasising both tails | Normal simulations with mean and sample SD refitted |

Use the provided functions as follows. This is a function-use example; apply it to all four series.

```{r}
#| eval: false
x <- daily$log_return[daily$asset == "Equities"]
daily_reference <- normal_mc_reference(n = length(x), B = 4999)
normal_tests(x, daily_reference)
```

Generate **one reference per sample size**. The same reference serves every asset at that frequency because fitted-normal statistics are invariant to location and scale. Do not reuse the daily reference for the monthly sample.

1. Produce daily and monthly tables of $n$, SW, JB and AD p-values for all four series.
2. Display very small p-values as `<0.0001`; use `format_p(p, B=4999)` for AD. An asterisk marks the smallest simulated value, $1/5000$, rather than a p-value of zero.
3. Add QQ plots of daily and monthly equities, standardised separately.
4. Compare the test results with your graphical diagnosis.
5. Explain any disagreement between tests, and what changed between frequencies.

**Write before opening the explanation:** “The monthly p-value is larger, therefore monthly returns are normal.” What is missing?

<details class="concept">
<summary>Show the interpretation guide.</summary>
<div class="answer"><p>Aggregation changes the return distribution, but it also reduces the sample from 1,510 to 71 observations. Tests may have less power. Non-rejection does not confirm normality. The reference also assumes independence and stable parameters, which these marginal plots and tests do not establish.</p></div>
</details>

Do not choose the largest p-value as a model-selection score or count tests as independent votes. These are related descriptive investigations; a formal search for multiple discoveries would need an explicit multiplicity procedure.

## Task 5: Why KS needs refitting

The observed KS statistic compares the empirical CDF with a normal CDF fitted to the same sample. A fair reference must reproduce that fitting step.

Use **monthly equities** and the supplied experiment:

```{r}
#| eval: false
x_month <- monthly$log_return[monthly$asset == "Equities"]
experiment <- ks_refit_experiment(x_month, B = 4999, seed = 209702)
experiment$p_values
```

Open `ks_refit_experiment()` in `week02_lab_helpers.R`. Identify the lines that:

1. fit the original mean and SD;
2. generate a new sample from those original parameters;
3. compare it with the original CDF;
4. refit mean and SD for the simulated comparison.

Then run the experiment and:

- plot the fixed-parameter and refitted reference statistics side by side, using common axes;
- mark the observed statistic on both panels;
- compare ordinary KS, fixed-parameter simulation and simulation with refitting;
- explain why the first two answer the wrong reference question here.

```{r}
# Run the experiment, plot its two reference distributions, and explain the p-values.

```

<details class="concept">
<summary>Which parameters remain fixed, and which must change?</summary>
<div class="answer"><p>The original estimates remain fixed as the generator of every bootstrap sample. Each new sample then gets its own estimates for calculating its discrepancy. Omitting that second fit compares the observed statistic with a different procedure, typically inflating the fitted-normal KS p-value.</p></div>
</details>

The correctly refitted p-value need not equal the lecture's simulated value exactly: the random seed is different. A useful scale for Monte Carlo error away from zero is $\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/B}$. The ordinary analytic KS value should agree for the identical sample.

## Task 6: A jump scenario with a financial mechanism

Use Merton's model to investigate occasional discrete repricing:

$$
r_h=ah+\sigma\sqrt h\,Z+\sum_{j=1}^{N_h}Y_j,\quad
N_h\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda h),\quad
Y_j\sim N(m_J,s_J^2).
$$

Here $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and the components are independent. The supplied `jump_model()` sets

$$
a=\mu-\sigma^2/2-\lambda\left(e^{m_J+s_J^2/2}-1\right),
\qquad E[e^{r_h}]=e^{\mu h}.
$$

Start with the lecture's **illustrative** annual parameters:
$\mu=8\%$, $\sigma=14\%$, $\lambda=2$, $m_J=-4\%$, $s_J=6\%$,
and horizon $h=1/252$ year.

```{r}
#| eval: false
base_model <- jump_model()
r_jump <- simulate_jump_returns(100000, base_model, seed = 209706)
```

1. Simulate the base scenario. Check the sample mean of `exp(r_jump)` against `base_model$expected_gross`, allowing for Monte Carlo error.
2. Simulate a normal comparator using `base_model$log_mean` and `sqrt(base_model$log_variance)`. These match the log moments, not necessarily expected wealth.
3. For each model, report the **one-day 0.1% and 99.9% simple-return quantiles**, and corresponding wealth quantiles for EUR 100,000. Use analytical normal quantiles and `jump_quantile()` as numerical checks.
4. **Predict first:** what changes if expected jump frequency rises from 2 to 4 per year? Set `jump_model(lambda=4)` and rerun the comparison. Recompute the matched normal comparator for the new scenario.
5. Explain why the helper must also change the drift $a$.
6. Identify one feature in an observed asset's QQ plot that makes jumps worth investigating. State one reason this exercise does not validate the model for that asset.

```{r}
# Base and higher-frequency scenarios, matched normal comparators, checks and quantiles.

```

<details class="concept">
<summary>What remains constant when lambda changes through jump_model()?</summary>
<div class="answer"><p>The chosen expected wealth growth remains exp(mu*h), because the drift correction changes with jump frequency. The distribution and its log moments can still change. A normal comparator matching those log moments must be recalculated.</p></div>
</details>

The extreme-quantile estimates use roughly 100 observations in each 0.1% tail when simulating 100,000 draws, so simulation uncertainty matters. Numerical model quantiles help separate simulation noise from model differences. Inspect both tails: a jump model need not give more extreme quantiles at every probability.

These are scenarios, not fitted models of the historical assets. Do not fit Student-t log returns: as discussed in the lecture, exponentiating them gives infinite expected wealth.

## Optional extensions

- **Weekly frequency:** repeat the comparison using `returns_weekly_eur.csv`. Check sample size before generating the reference.
- **A different discrepancy:** inspect CvM and refitted KS results already returned by `normal_tests()`. Explain how they differ from AD without treating p-values as a ranking.
- **Write the bootstrap:** implement a short refitting loop yourself, then compare it with the helper using the same seed and statistic.
- **Time ordering:** shuffle equity returns and compare the original and shuffled plots. Verify that moments and normality-test statistics remain unchanged although the time pattern changes.
- **Combined D’Agostino–Pearson:** research a documented implementation of the combined $K^2$ test and its sample-size conditions before using it. Identify the skewness and kurtosis components. This is not required for the core lab.
